value.overview: The Rusty Sparrow (Aimophila rufescens) is a medium-sized New World sparrow of Mexico and Central America. It is named for its warm reddish-brown crown and rusty tones in the wings and back. The species usually stays near the ground in brushy, open woodland rather than deep forest. In Costa Rica it is a localized bird of the northwestern Pacific region, especially the Guanacaste highlands and volcanic slopes.
value.classification: The Rusty Sparrow belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows. It is one of several closely related sparrows in the genus Aimophila.
value.identification: This sparrow is about 17–20 cm long. Adults have a rusty or reddish-brown crown, grayish face and upper breast, a pale throat marked with dark streaking, and brown wings and tail with subdued rufous edges. A pale eye-ring may be visible. The combination of a rusty cap, gray face, streaked throat, and brushland habitat helps separate it from other Costa Rican sparrows.
value.rangeHabitat: The Rusty Sparrow ranges from Mexico south through parts of Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is localized mainly on the Pacific side of Guanacaste, including the Cordillera de Guanacaste and nearby volcanic slopes. It uses dry forest, pine-oak or oak woodland, wooded scrub, forest edges, second growth, clearings, and brushy rocky hillsides, generally from low to middle elevations and locally higher.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident, including in Costa Rica. There is no reliable evidence that Costa Rican birds undertake regular long-distance migration, although local movements may follow food and habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The Rusty Sparrow nests close to the ground, using sites in grass, brush, or earthen banks, sometimes beside paths or other open areas. The nest is a small cup made from grasses and other plant fibers. Breeding information is less thoroughly documented than for many widespread sparrows, and timing varies across its broad range. In Costa Rica, breeding is associated with suitable brushy habitat in the northwestern Pacific region.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of seeds and other plant material, supplemented by insects and other small invertebrates, particularly when feeding young. It usually searches on the ground or among low shrubs, moving deliberately through leaf litter, grasses, and open brush. Pairs or small family groups may forage together, and the species often remains concealed until it is flushed or begins calling.
value.behavior: The Rusty Sparrow is a secretive, mostly terrestrial songbird that commonly moves through dense low vegetation. It may occur alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. When disturbed, it often slips into cover rather than flying far. Its song and calls are useful for detection because the bird can be difficult to see in brush. In Costa Rica it is localized and may be uncommon even within its limited range.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is not currently considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline for a threatened category.
